newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr rallies as RBA cools rate talk.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr rallies as RBA cools rate talk.

text.p: The Australian dollar blipped higher in late Tuesday trading after Reserve Bank Governor Ian Macfarlane all but ruled out a near term easing in policy.

Asked about the outlook for monetary policy after a speech in Sydney, Macfarlane said the bank felt some effects were being seen from the three rate cuts already delivered and the outlook for the economy in 1997 was better than 1996.

He said that the bank had to look at inflation from a long term perspective and therefore with some important developments on wages coming up it was only logical to wait until the results of those developments were known.
By 8.00 pm (0900 GMT) the local dollar had climbed to US$0.7615/20 from US$0.7570/75 just before Macfarlane's words hit dealing screens.
Referring to inflation, Macfarlane said the bank had to take account of data that had effects stretching out over more than a year and a half.

"When we do that of course developments in the wages data form an important part of that, so if you have some important information on this from the market sector or the administered sector, then it would be only logical to wait until you saw what the results were," he said.

Analysts interpreted that to mean the bank was prepared to await developments on wages, and in particular how a minimum wages claim currently being considered by the Industrial Relations Commission (IRC), turned out.
The bank has repeatedly criticised the union claim as being unrealistically high and incompatible with the maintenance of the bank's 2-3 percent underlying inflation target.
Macfarlane himself has warned that if administered wage settlements became more wide ranging, the bank may eventually have to respond to rising inflationary pressures by raising rates.
The union claim is for an 8.75 pay rise for the low-paid and for three A$20 a week net rises in safety net, or minimum, wages over the next three years.

Crucially, the IRC, which is an independent body, is not expected to make its ruling until the start of March at the earliest. Analysts therefore concluded that the RBA would not be considering another easing until the ruling was known and not at all if the full or larger part of the claim was granted.
Equally, Macfarlane's optimism on the economy also pointed to a willingness to wait and see how the impacts of the 150 basis points of easing already delivered fed through.
"Our feeling is that some of the effects are coming through," Macfarlane said about the last three cuts.
He said the sort of economic information received over the last couple of months was better than that during the second half of 1996 when the bank was cutting rates.

He put an emphasis on business investment and a turnaround in the housing sector, and also noted that employment growth had picked up in the second half of last year. ""There was an implication the bank is prepared to wait and see whether this improvement can be sustained before any further policy action was taken," said Westpac economist Bill Evans.
Evans, general manager economic strategy and planning at Westpac, said this was consistent with his view that the bank was ready to delay any action on policy.
"Macfalane's latest comments are further support for our view that it is unlikely the bank will change interest rates throughout the course of 1997," said Evans.
The money market seemed to agree and knocked seven basis points off the March bank bill future to 94.09, implying little change was now expected from the present official cash rate of 6.0 percent.
